This notebook is an exploratory analysis of the differential expression of proteins in spheroid proteomics data. The analysis is performed on the global proteomics data, and the results are visualized using PCA plots and heatmaps. The analysis is performed on the MN4, WU225, and JHU2002 spheroids, with an optional inclusion of the MN2 spheroid.

# Library & Data import

Depending on the directory this notebook is run / knitted from, the path to the source code and output directory may need to be adjusted. The default paths assume that this notebook is run from the `notebooks` directory.

As an additional optional dataset we can include MN2 into the data (more on that in [Optional inclusion of MN2](#sec-optional-inclusion-of-mn2)). To make this step optional we will use a boolean variable `eval_mn2` to control whether or not the MN2 data is included in the analysis. If `eval_mn2` is set to `TRUE`, we will retrieve and clean up the MN2 data, and if it is set to `FALSE`, we will skip this step. Additionally we will store every generated figure into a separate output directory, which will be created if it does not exist.

```{r}
#| label: eval_mn2

eval_mn2 <- TRUE

if (!eval_mn2) {
  cat("MN2 data will not be included in the analysis.")
} else {
  cat("MN2 data will be included in the analysis.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: path-setup

src_dir <- "../src/"
output_dir_root <- "../output_figures/"

if (!dir.exists(output_dir_root)) {
  stop(paste0("Root of output directory does not exist: ", output_dir_root))
}

if (!eval_mn2) {
  output_dir <- paste0(output_dir_root, "batch2_differential_expression/")
} else {
  output_dir <- paste0(
    output_dir_root,
    "batch2_differential_expression_including_MN2/"
  )
}
if (!dir.exists(output_dir)) {
  dir.create(output_dir)
}
```

```{r}
sc <- import("synapseclient")
```

Then we can use the functionality from the `synapseclient` package to retrieve the data files from Synapse. The data files include the global proteomics abundance data and the associated meta data.

```{r}
syn <- sc$Synapse()

# getting the global proteomics abundance data
synapseFileID <- "syn77329971"
fileEntity <- syn$get(synapseFileID)
global_dat <- readr::read_tsv(

meta_dat <- read_xlsx(fileEntity$path, sheet = "Combined")

```

```{r}
#| label: data-summary
head(global_dat)
head(meta_dat)
```

# Data preparation generation of the `SummarizedExperiment` object

## MN4, WU225, and JHU2002 spheroids

As this notebook is focused primarily on the MN4, WU225, and JHU2002 spheroids, we will spend some time and provide more detail on the data preparation steps for these spheroids. The optional data preparation steps for the MN2 spheroid are similar, and will be described in a separate section.

### Proteomics data cleanup

As we could see from the summary, the global proteomics data has a number of columns with file paths and other information that we don't need for our analysis. We will clean up the column names to make them more informative and easier to work with. Additionally we remove a few columns that are not needed for our analysis, such as the first protein description and the number of sequences and proteotypic sequences.
```{r}
#| label: proteomics-data-cleanup
#| 

# cleaning up the column names for the global proteomics data
names(global_dat) %<>%
  gsub("D:\\\\Data_D\\\\LeDay\\\\Spheroid_7863\\\\rawdata\\\\", "", .) %>%
  gsub("^[0-9]*_MPNST_spheroid_3Patient_", "", .) %>%
  gsub("_Maggie_50SPD_[0-9]+Aug[0-9]+_ES906-3408_[0-9]*.raw", "", .)


global_dat %<>%
  dplyr::select(
    -c('First.Protein.Description', 'N.Sequences', 'N.Proteotypic.Sequences')
  )
```

### Meta data cleanup

Then we do the same thing for the meta data, cleaning up the column names and creating new columns for downstream analysis. We also create a new column that combines the spheroid, timepoint, and agent information into a single string, which will be useful for grouping samples in our analysis.

```{r}
#| label: meta-data-cleanup

# getting the new column names for the meta data
new_col_names <- c(
  global_sample_id = "Proteomics Sample ID",
  # phospho_sample_id = "Phosphoproteomics Sample ID",
  agent = "Drug",
  timepoint = "Time",
  plate = "Plate",
  spheroid = "Speroid"
)

# cleaning up sample ids in meta data
meta_dat$`Proteomics Sample ID` %<>% str_sub(., 23)

# renaming columns in meta data and creating new columns for downstream analysis
meta_dat %<>%
  dplyr::rename(., all_of(new_col_names)) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(plate_by_spheroid = paste(spheroid, plate, sep = "_")) %>%
  mutate(agent = gsub(" ", "", agent), timepoint = paste0(timepoint, "hr")) %>%
  mutate(group = paste(spheroid, timepoint, agent, sep = "_")) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  mutate(replicate = paste0('r', 1:n())) %>%
  mutate(
    condition = paste(spheroid, timepoint, agent, replicate, sep = '_')
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

meta_data_global <- meta_dat %>%
  select(., global_sample_id, condition, plate_by_spheroid) %>%
  dplyr::rename(., sample = global_sample_id) %>%
  dplyr::rename(., plate = plate_by_spheroid)

```

## Optional inclusion of MN2

As an additional optional spheroid we can include the MN2 spheroid in our analysis. The data for this spheroid is stored in separate files on Synapse, and we will need to retrieve and clean up the data in a similar way as we did for the other spheroids. 

The following code chunks provide the steps for retrieving and cleaning up the MN2 data, similar to what we did for the other spheroids. We will retrieve the global proteomics data and meta data for the MN2 spheroid from Synapse, clean up the column names, and create new columns for downstream analysis.

```{r}
#| label: synapse-file-retrieval-mn2
#| warning: false
#| error: false

if (!eval_mn2) {
  cat("MN2 data will not be included in the analysis.")
} else {
  syn <- sc$Synapse()
  syn$login(silent = TRUE)

  # getting the global proteomics abundance data
  synapseFileID <- "syn74552028"
  fileEntity <- syn$get(synapseFileID)
  mn2_global_dat <- readr::read_tsv(
    fileEntity$path,
    na = c("0", "", NA), # the file stored on synapse has '0's instead of NA or ''
  )

  # getting the meta data
  synapseFileID <- "syn74755705"
  fileEntity <- syn$get(synapseFileID)
  mn2_meta_dat <- read_xlsx(fileEntity$path, sheet = 2)

  syn$logout()

  names(mn2_global_dat) <- names(mn2_global_dat) %>%
    gsub("D:\\\\Data_D\\\\LeDay\\\\spheroid_MN02\\\\rawdata\\\\", "", .) %>%
    gsub("_16Apr26_Monty_ES906_2014_50SPD[x]*.raw", "", .) %>%
    gsub("^[0-9]*_cNF_spheroid_", "G_", .)

  mn2_global_dat %<>%
    dplyr::select(
      -c('First.Protein.Description', 'N.Sequences', 'N.Proteotypic.Sequences')
    )

  new_col_names <- c(
    sample = 'Sample ID \r\n(abbrev)',
    global_sample_id = "Proteomics Sample ID",
    phospho_sample_id = "Phosphoproteomics Sample ID",
    agent = "Drug",
    timepoint = "Time",
    plate = "Plate"
  )

  mn2_meta_dat %<>%
    rowwise() %>%
    mutate(Drug = gsub(" ", "", Drug), Time = paste0(Time, "hr")) %>%
    mutate(spheroid = "MN2") %>%
    mutate(group = paste(Time, Drug, sep = "_")) %>%
    mutate(Plate = paste(spheroid, Plate, sep = "_")) %>%
    group_by(group) %>%
    mutate(replicate = paste0('r', 1:n())) %>%
    mutate(condition = paste(spheroid, Time, Drug, replicate, sep = '_')) %>%
    dplyr::rename(., all_of(new_col_names)) %>%
    ungroup()
}
```

One crucial difference between the MN2 dataset and the other spheroid dataset is that we have proteomics data for a larger set of drugs that the MN2 spheroid has been treated with. To ensure that we are only including the drugs that are also present in the other spheroid datasets, we will filter the MN2 data to only include the drugs that are present in the meta data for the other spheroids. We know that the drugs that are present in the other spheroid datasets are *DMSO* (the control), *Mirda*, *Palbo*, *TNO155*, and *Vorino* at the *8h*, *24h* and *48h* time points. The corresponding plates for the MN2 spheroid are *MN2_1*, *MN2_4*, and *MN2_6*. We will filter the MN2 meta data to only include these plates, and then we will select the corresponding columns from the MN2 global proteomics data.

```{r}
#| label: proteomics-data-cleanup-mn2-select-cols
if (!eval_mn2) {
  cat("MN2 data will not be included in the analysis.")
} else {
  mn2_meta_dat <- mn2_meta_dat[
    mn2_meta_dat$plate %in% c("MN2_1", "MN2_4", "MN2_6"),
  ]

  mn2_meta_data_global <- mn2_meta_dat %>%
    select(., global_sample_id, condition, plate) %>%
    dplyr::rename(., sample = global_sample_id) %>%
    mutate(sample = gsub("cNF_spheroid_", "G_", sample))

  cols_to_keep <- c(
    'Protein.Group',
    'Protein.Names',
    'Genes',
    mn2_meta_data_global$sample
  )
  mn2_global_dat %<>%
    dplyr::select(all_of(cols_to_keep))
}
```

Finally we will combine both the meta data and the global proteomics data for the MN2 spheroid with the meta data and global proteomics data for the other spheroids. This will allow us to generate one combined `SummarizedExperiment` object that includes all of the spheroids and drugs that we are interested in analyzing. We will use a full join to combine the data, which will ensure that we keep all of the proteins and samples from both datasets.

```{r}
#| label: combine-mn2-data
#| 
if (!eval_mn2) {
  cat("MN2 data will not be included in the analysis.")
} else {
  global_dat %<>%
    full_join(
      .,
      mn2_global_dat,
      by = c('Protein.Group', 'Protein.Names', 'Genes')
    )

  meta_data_global %<>%
    rbind(
      .,
      mn2_meta_data_global
    )
}
```

# Dataset overview
As a first step, we will perform a PCA analysis on the global proteomics data to get an overview of the dataset. PCA is a dimensionality reduction technique that allows us to visualize the variation in the data and identify any potential outliers or batch effects. To that end we will first prepare the data for PCA analysis using the `prep_experiment_data` function. This function takes in the proteomics data, meta data, and various parameters for filtering and imputation, and returns a list of `SummarizedExperiment` objects that can be used for downstream analysis.

Importantly we set the `missingness_cutoff` to 0 and the `imputation_method` to 'SampMin'. This means that we will not filter out any proteins based on missingness, and we will impute missing values using the sample minimum method. The imputation is needed for PCA analysis, as PCA cannot be performed on data with missing values. We also set the `samp_cutoff` to 0 for both global and phospho data, meaning that we will not filter out any samples based on missingness.

```{r}
#| label: prep-data-for-pca-overview
prot_data <- list()
meta_data <- list()

prot_data[['global']] <- global_dat
meta_data[['global']] <- meta_data_global

experiment <- prepare_proteomics_data(
  proteomics_data = prot_data[['global']],
  proteomics_meta = meta_data[['global']],
  type = 'global',
  imputation_method = 'SampMin',
  sample_col_prefix = "G_",
  group_contains_spheroid = TRUE
)
```

Then we can generate a PCA plot for the global proteomics data using the `plot_pca` function. This function takes in a `SummarizedExperiment` object and various parameters for coloring, shaping, and labeling the samples, and returns a ggplot object that can be visualized or saved to a file. We will color the samples by agent, and shape them by timepoint. We will also add ellipses to the plot to indicate the grouping of samples by spheroid.

```{r}
#| label: plot-pca-overview
#| warning: false

colors <- list(
  "DMSO" = color_vals_black_first[1],
  "Mirda" = color_vals_black_first[2],
  "Palbo" = color_vals_black_first[3],
  "TNO155" = color_vals_black_first[5],
  "Vorino" = color_vals_black_first[7]
)

plot <- plot_pca(
  experiment,
  color_by = 'agent',
  shape_by = 'timepoint',
  title = "Global proteomics PCA",
  color_vals = colors
)
plot <- plot +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group = spheroid, linetype = spheroid), color = "darkgrey") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

plot
```

Optionally we can save the PCA plot to a file in the output directory.

```{r}
#| label: save-pca-overview
#| eval: !expr params$saveplots

fname <- paste0(output_dir, "batch2_overview_pca.pdf")

ggsave(
  filename = fname,
  plot = plot,
  height = 6,
  width = 8
)
```

As we can see from the PCA plot, as expected there is a clear separation of the samples based on the spheroid that they were derived from. There is also some separation based on the agent and timepoint, but this is less pronounced. Just to get a slighthly better overview we will generate individual PCA plots per spheroid.

```{r}
#| label: plot-pca-overview-per-spheroid

spheroids <- as_tibble(colData(experiment)) %>% pull(spheroid) %>% unique()

plots <- list()
for (spheroid in spheroids) {
  plot <- plot_pca(
    experiment,
    subset_by = 'spheroid',
    subset_values = spheroid,
    color_by = 'agent',
    shape_by = 'timepoint',
    color_vals = colors,
    # label_by = 'condition',
    title = paste0("Global proteomics PCA for ", spheroid)
  )
  plot <- plot +
    stat_ellipse(
      aes(group = timepoint, linetype = timepoint),
      color = "darkgrey"
    ) +
    theme(legend.position = "right")

  plots[[spheroid]] <- plot
  print(plot)
}
```

Optionally we can save the individual PCA plots for each spheroid to files in the output directory.
```{r}
#| label: save-pca-overview-per-spheroid-plots
#| eval: !expr params$saveplots

for (spheroid in names(plots)) {
  ggsave(
    filename = paste0(output_dir, "batch2_overview_pca_", spheroid, ".png"),
    plot = plots[[spheroid]],
    height = 4,
    width = 5
  )
}
```

Investigating the individual PCA plots it is very clear that the driving factor for the separation of the samples per spheroid is the timepoint. This is especially true for the MN4 and specifically the WU225 spheroids. Given the fact that the timepoint also correlates to the plate that the samples were processed on, it is likely that this separation is due to a batch effect. We need to keep this in mind for later downstream analysis, if we want to invesigate differential expression across timepoints.

The other observation we can make from the PCA plots is that there are some outlier samples that are separated from the main cluster of samples. These outliers may need to be removed from the analysis, as they could be driving the separation of the samples and potentially biasing the results. We will investigate these outliers further in the next section.

# Missingness and outlier investigation

The first thing we want to do is to investigate the missingness in our data. Missingness can be a problem in proteomics data, as it can lead to biased results if not handled properly. We will look at the distribution of missing values across samples and proteins, and identify any outliers that may need to be removed from the analysis.

Since we specifically want to investigate missingness, we set the `missingness_cutoff` to 0 and the `imputation_method` to 'none'. This means that we will not filter out any proteins based on missingness, and we will not perform any imputation on the data.
```{r}
#| label: prep-data-for-missingness-investigation

experiment <- prepare_proteomics_data(
  proteomics_data = prot_data[['global']],
  proteomics_meta = meta_data[['global']],
  type = 'global',
  sample_col_prefix = "G_",
  group_contains_spheroid = TRUE
)
```

## Missingness distribution

With the data prepared, we can now look at the distribution of missing values across proteins. First, we calculate the missingness for each protein as the proportion of samples in which the protein is missing. We then calculate the z-score of the missingness values to identify outliers. 

Finally, we return the number of outlier proteins and the minimum missingness value among the outliers. This information can be used to set a threshold for filtering out proteins with high missingness in downstream analysis. As comparison, we also return the number of proteins with missingness greater than the 75th percentile of the missingness distribution. This gives us an idea of how many proteins have relatively high missingness, even if they are not considered outliers based on the z-score.

```{r}
#| label: calculate-missingness-outliers

pdat <- assay(experiment)
p_missingness <- enframe(
  rowSums(is.na(pdat)) / ncol(pdat),
  name = 'protein',
  value = 'missingness'
)

p_missingness$outlier <- get_zscore_outliers(
  p_missingness$missingness,
  sensitivity = 3,
  sided = 'right'
)

p_missingness$outlier_less_sensitive <- get_zscore_outliers(
  p_missingness$missingness,
  sensitivity = 2,
  sided = 'right'
)

cat(paste0(
  "Outliers (Z > 3): ",
  length(p_missingness$protein[p_missingness$outlier]),
  "\n",
  "Outliers (Z > 2): ",
  length(p_missingness$protein[p_missingness$outlier_less_sensitive])
))

z_score_based_missingness_cutoffs <- c(
  'Z > 3' = min(p_missingness$missingness[
    p_missingness$outlier
  ]),
  'Z > 2' = min(p_missingness$missingness[
    p_missingness$outlier_less_sensitive
  ])
)

cat(paste0(
  "Outliers (missingness > 75th percentile): ",
  dim(p_missingness[
    p_missingness$missingness > quantile(p_missingness$missingness)[4],
  ])[1]
))
```

As we can see the number of outlier proteins based on the z-score of missingness is relatively small (_`r length(p_missingness$protein[p_missingness$outlier_less_sensitive])`_), and the minimum missingness value among the outliers is _`r z_score_based_missingness_cutoffs['Z > 2']`_. Compared to the number of proteins with missingness greater than the 75th percentile of the missingness distribution (_`r dim(p_missingness[p_missingness$missingness > quantile(p_missingness$missingness)[4],])[1]`_), the number of outlier proteins is much smaller.

For now we will use the z-score based cutoff for filtering out proteins with high missingness in downstream analysis.

We then can visualize the distribution of missingness across proteins using a histogram and density plot. We also add vertical dashed lines to indicate the cutoff for outlier proteins based on the z-score of missingness.

```{r}
#| label: plot-missingness-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of missingness across proteins. The vertical dashed line indicates the cutoff for outlier proteins based on the z-score of missingness."
#| 

plot <- p_missingness %$%
  (ggplot(., aes(x = missingness)) +
    geom_histogram(
      aes(y = after_stat(density)),
      bins = 100,
      fill = 'lightgrey'
    ) +
    geom_density(color = 'black') +
    geom_vline(
      xintercept = z_score_based_missingness_cutoffs,
      linetype = 'dashed',
      color = c('Z > 3' = 'red', 'Z > 2' = 'orange')
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(
      title = "Distribution of missingness across proteins",
      x = "Missingness (proportion of samples with missing values)",
      y = "Density"
    ) +
    annotate(
      "text",
      x = z_score_based_missingness_cutoffs,
      y = -2,
      label = paste0(
        c("Z > 3", "Z > 2"),
        ": ",
        round(z_score_based_missingness_cutoffs, 2)
      ),
      color = c('Z > 3' = 'red', 'Z > 2' = 'orange'),
      hjust = -0.1
    ))

plot
```

Finally, we save the plot to a file in the output directory. (Note that the `eval` option is set to `false` for this code chunk, so the plot will not be generated when the notebook is run.)

```{r}
#| label: save-missingness-distribution-plot
#| eval: !expr params$saveplots

ggsave(
  filename = paste0(output_dir, "batch2_missingness_distribution.png"),
  plot = plot,
  height = 3,
  width = 5
)
```

## Missingness per plate (Spheroid)

Next we want to look at the missingness per plate (spheroid) to see if there are any plates with unusually high missingness. We will use the `plot_per_plate_na_overview` function to generate a bar plot showing the number of missing values per plate for each protein type (global and phospho). The function takes in a `SummarizedExperiment` object and the protein type as input, and returns a ggplot object.

```{r}
#| label: plot-missingness-per-plate

# add a comparison between the NAs without missingness removal and with missingness removal

plot <- plot_per_plate_na_overview(experiment, 'global')
print(plot)
```

Finally, we save the plot to a file in the output directory. (Note that the `eval` option is set to `false` for this code chunk, so the plot will not be generated when the notebook is run.)
```{r}
#| label: save-missingness-per-plate-plot
#| eval: !expr params$saveplots
ggsave(
  filename = paste0(output_dir, "batch2_missingness_outliers_per_plate.png"),
  plot = plot,
  height = 4,
  width = 6
)
```

As we can see from the plot some plates show a few samples with unusually high missingness. The outlier detection here is directly done by the box-plot function and for consistency we want to use the previously used z-score based outlier detection method. 

Below we will calculate the number of missing values per sample and identify any outliers based on the z-score of the number of missing values. Importantly we are still only interested on those samples with high missingness, hence we set `sided = "right"`. We will then return a table showing the sample ID, plate, and number of missing values for any outlier samples.

```{r}
summarized_data <- as_tibble(assay(experiment)) %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "sample_id", values_to = "NAs")

metadata <- colData(experiment) %>%
  as.data.frame(.) %>%
  rownames_to_column(., var = "sample_id") %>%
  as_tibble(.)

data <- inner_join(metadata, summarized_data, by = 'sample_id') %>%
  group_by(plate) %>%
  mutate(
    outlier = get_zscore_outliers(NAs, sensitivity = 2, sided = "right")
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(
    .,
    -one_of(c("condition", "group", "plate"))
  )

data[data$outlier == TRUE, ]
```

We now can use the gathered information about the missingness distribution and the outlier samples to set a threshold for filtering out proteins with high missingness in downstream analysis. We will use the z-score based cutoff for filtering out proteins with high missingness, and we will remove any outlier samples identified based on the z-score of the number of missing values.

# PCA plots (Spheroid)

Now that we have determined the missingness cutoff for filtering out proteins with high missingness, we can prepare the data for PCA analysis. We will use the `prep_experiment_data` function again, this time with the `missingness_cutoff` set to the z-score based cutoff we determined earlier, and the `imputation_method` set to "SampMin". This means that we will filter out proteins with missingness greater than the cutoff, and we will impute missing values using the sample minimum method.

```{r}
#| label: prep-data-for-pca

f_missingness_cutoff <- z_score_based_missingness_cutoffs['Z > 2']
s_to_exclude <- data[data$outlier == TRUE, ] %>% pull(sample_id)

experiment <- prepare_proteomics_data(
  proteomics_data = prot_data[['global']],
  proteomics_meta = meta_data[['global']],
  type = 'global',
  sample_col_prefix = "G_",
  group_contains_spheroid = TRUE,
  feature_missingness_cutoff = f_missingness_cutoff,
  samples_to_exclude = s_to_exclude,
  imputation_method = "SampMin"
)
```

## PCA plots per plate (Spheroid)

Next we generate PCA plots for each plate (spheroid) and protein type (global and phospho - note phospho data is currently not being investigated). We will use the `plot_pca_by_plate` function to generate the PCA plots.

```{r}
#| label: plot-pca-by-plate

plots <- list()
colors <- list(
  "DMSO" = color_vals_black_first[1],
  "Mirda" = color_vals_black_first[2],
  "Palbo" = color_vals_black_first[3],
  "TNO155" = color_vals_black_first[5],
  "Vorino" = color_vals_black_first[7]
)

colData(experiment)$label <- paste(
  colData(experiment)$agent,
  colData(experiment)$replicate,
  sep = '_'
)
plates <- as_tibble(colData(experiment)) %>% pull(plate) %>% unique()
for (plate in plates) {
  spheroid <- as_tibble(colData(experiment[, experiment$plate == plate])) %>%
    pull(spheroid) %>%
    unique()
  timepoint <- as_tibble(colData(experiment[, experiment$plate == plate])) %>%
    pull(timepoint) %>%
    unique()
  title <- paste0("Global proteomics for ", spheroid, " at ", timepoint)

  plot <- plot_pca(
    experiment,
    subset_by = 'plate',
    subset_values = plate,
    color_by = 'agent',
    shape_by = 'agent',
    # label_by = 'label',
    color_vals = colors,
    title = title
  )
  plots[[plate]] <- plot
  print(plot)
}
```

Then we save the PCA plots for each plate (spheroid) and protein type (global and phospho - note phosphodata is currently not being investigated) to files in the output directory. (Note that the `eval` option is set to `false` for this code chunk, so the plots will not be generated when the notebook is run.)
```{r}
#| label: save-pca-by-plate-plots
#| eval: !expr params$saveplots

for (prot_type in c('global')) {
  plates <- as_tibble(colData(experiment)) %>% pull(plate) %>% unique()
  for (plate in plates) {
    fname <- paste0(
      output_dir,
      "batch2_pca_",
      prot_type,
      "_by_plate_",
      plate,
      ".png"
    )
    ggsave(fname, plot = plots[[plate]], height = 5, width = 5)
  }
}
```

# Differential expression analysis
Now that we have a good overview of the dataset, we can move on to the differential expression analysis. We will use the `plot_diff_ex` function to generate volcano plots for each agent and timepoint, comparing the treated samples to the control samples. 

```{r}
agents <- c('Mirda', 'TNO155', 'Palbo', 'Vorino')
timepoints <- c("8hr", "24hr", "48hr")
log_fc <- .5
pval <- 0.1

plots <- list()
plots_agents <- list()

for (spheroid in spheroids) {
  for (agent in agents) {
    for (timepoint in timepoints) {
      experiment_subset <- experiment[,
        experiment$agent %in%
          c(agent, "DMSO") &
          experiment$timepoint == timepoint
      ]

      plots[[spheroid]][[agent]][[timepoint]] <- plot_diff_ex(
        experiment_subset,
        agent,
        timepoint,
        log_fc = log_fc,
        pval = pval,
        prot_type = 'global',
        spheroid = spheroid
      )
      plot_title <- paste(
        spheroid,
        'global proteomics:',
        agent,
        "vs. Control"
      )
    }
    plots_agents[[spheroid]][[agent]] <- plot_diff_ex_grid(
      plots[[spheroid]][[agent]],
      plot_title
    )
    print(plots_agents[[spheroid]][[agent]])
  }
}
```


And as always we will save the plots to files in the output directory. (Note that the `eval` option is set to `false` for this code chunk, so the plots will not be generated when the notebook is run.)
```{r}
#| label: save-diff-ex-plots
#| eval: !expr params$saveplots

agents <- c('Mirda', 'TNO155', 'Palbo', 'Vorino')
for (agent in agents) {
  for (spheroid in spheroids) {
    fname <- paste0(
      output_dir,
      "batch2_diff-ex_",
      "global-proteomics_",
      agent,
      "_",
      spheroid,
      ".png"
    )
    ggsave(
      fname,
      plot = plots_agents[[spheroid]][[agent]],
      height = 5,
      width = 7
    )
  }
}
```

# Pathway enrichment analysis

Now we take the "most interesting" result from the differential expression analysis and perform pathway enrichment analysis on it. This will allow us to identify any biological pathways that are significantly enriched in the differentially expressed proteins, which can provide insights into the underlying biological processes affected by the treatments.

## Data preparation

As a first step we will generate the differential expression results for all agents and timepoints, and store them in a list for downstream analysis. We will use the `calc_diff_ex` function to calculate the differential expression results, which takes in a `SummarizedExperiment` object, the names of the two groups to compare, and various parameters for filtering and adjusting the results.

Since we are dealing only with drugs (agents) that have a DMSO control, we will use DMSO as the control group for all comparisons. We will also set the `align_by` parameter to `"Protein.Group"`, which is the unified protein identifier used in the global proteomics data.

```{r}
#| label: calc-diff-ex-for-pathway-enrichment

all_diff_ex <- list()
ctrl <- "DMSO"

for (spheroid in spheroids) {
  for (agent in agents) {
    for (timepoint in timepoints) {
      experiment_subset <- experiment[,
        experiment$agent %in%
          c(agent, ctrl) &
          experiment$timepoint == timepoint
      ]

      group_1 <- paste0(spheroid, "_", timepoint, "_", ctrl)
      group_2 <- paste0(spheroid, "_", timepoint, "_", agent)

      diff_ex <- calc_diff_ex(
        experiment_subset,
        group_1,
        group_2,
        align_by = "Protein.Group"
      )

      all_diff_ex[[spheroid]][[agent]][[timepoint]] <- diff_ex
    }
  }
}
```

## Pathway enrichment plots
Now we can perform the run the pathway enrichment analysis. To get an overview of the enriched pathways, we will generate bar plots for each agent and timepoint, showing the top enriched pathways based on the adjusted p-value. We will use the `plot_leapr_bar` function to generate the bar plots, which takes in the results of the pathway enrichment analysis and various parameters for customizing the plot.

But first we need to load the necessary data for the pathway enrichment analysis. We will use the `ncipid` and `krbpaths` datasets from the `leapR` package, which contain information about pathways and their associated proteins.

```{r}
#| label: load-pathway-enrichment-data
data("ncipid")
data("krbpaths")
```

We will also set up some global parmeters for the pathway enrichment analysis, including the log fold change and p-value cutoffs for selecting differentially expressed proteins.

```{r}
#| label: pathway-enrichment-parameters
log_fc <- 0.5
pval <- 0.1
geneset <- ncipid
id_column <- "Genes"
```

Now we can generate the individual bar plots for each agent and timepoint, showing the top enriched pathways based on the adjusted p-value. We will store the plots in a list for later use where we will combine the plots for each spheroid and agent into a single plot. 

```{r}
#| label: pathway-enrichment-analysis

plots <- list()

for (spheroid in spheroids) {
  for (agent in agents) {
    for (timepoint in timepoints) {
      tryCatch(
        {
          enriched_pathways <- leapR(
            geneset = geneset,
            eset = all_diff_ex[[spheroid]][[agent]][[timepoint]],
            enrichment_method = "enrichment_in_sets",
            assay_name = 'proteomics',
            id_column = id_column,
            primary_column = "adj.P.Val",
            threshold = pval,
            greaterthan = FALSE
          )
          plot <- plot_leapr_bar(
            enriched_pathways,
            paste0(spheroid, ": ", agent, ' at ', timepoint)
          )
          plots[[spheroid]][[agent]][[timepoint]] <- plot
        },
        error = function(msg) {
          message(
            paste0(
              "pval of '",
              pval,
              "' did not result in differentially expressed proteins for agent '",
              agent,
              "' at timepoint '",
              timepoint,
              "'"
            )
          )
          return(NA)
        }
      )
    }
  }
}
```

Once the individual plots are generated, we can combine them into a single plot for each spheroid and agent, showing the top enriched pathways across all timepoints. We will use the `plot_layout` function from the `patchwork` package to arrange the individual plots in a grid layout.

```{r}
#| label: combine-pathway-enrichment-plots

combined_plots <- list()
for (spheroid in spheroids) {
  for (agent in agents) {
    plot_combined <- plots[[spheroid]][[agent]][[timepoints[1]]] +
      plots[[spheroid]][[agent]][[timepoints[2]]] +
      plots[[spheroid]][[agent]][[timepoints[3]]] +
      plot_layout(nrow = 3) # +
    # plot_annotation(
    #   title = paste0(spheroid, ": ", agent),
    #   theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14))
    # )
    combined_plots[[spheroid]][[agent]] <- plot_combined
    print(plot_combined)
  }
}
```

```{r}
#| label: save-pathway-enrichment-plots
for (spheroid in spheroids) {
  for (agent in agents) {
    fname <- paste0(
      output_dir,
      "batch2_pathway_enrichment_",
      "global-proteomics_",
      spheroid,
      "_",
      agent,
      ".png"
    )
    ggsave(
      fname,
      plot = combined_plots[[spheroid]][[agent]],
      width = 12,
      height = 10
    )
  }
}

```

After getting the overview of the enriched pathways across all spheroids, agents, and timepoints, we can see that one of the agents that shows the highest number of enriched pathways across spheroids is Mirda. We will now focus on the Mirda agent and generate a combined plot for all spheroids at the 48hr timepoint, which shows the top enriched pathways based on the adjusted p-value.

```{r}
#| label: combine-pathway-enrichment-mirda-plot

plot_combined_mirda_spheroids <- plots[['MN4']][['TNO155']][[timepoints[3]]] +
  plots[['WU225']][['TNO155']][[timepoints[3]]] +
  plots[['JHU2002']][['TNO155']][[timepoints[3]]] +
  plot_layout(nrow = 3) # +

plot_combined_mirda_spheroids
```

And as always we will save the combined plot for Mirda at the 48hr timepoint across all spheroids to a file in the output directory.

```{r}
#| label: save-pathway-enrichment-combined-mirda-plot
#| eval: !expr params$saveplots

ggsave(
  paste0(
    output_dir,
    "batch2_pathway_enrichment_global-proteomics_Mirda_48hr.png"
  ),
  plot = plot_combined_mirda_spheroids,
  width = 12,
  height = 10
)
```
